guides.title: Executive OS: principles, rules and routines
guides.definition: An executive operating system is a written arrangement of priorities, decision rules and recurring reviews for managing work. It connects what matters to the next action and records what happened afterward. Spry uses the term for a personal planning method, which can be run on paper or with an AI assistant.
guides.best_for: operators who have several planning tools but no agreed way to choose and finish the next task.
steps: Write the outcome you are responsible for in language someone else could verify. Separate a deliverable from an aspiration such as being more productive.
Choose a decision rule for competing requests. For example, protect an existing client deadline before starting an optional internal improvement.
Give the priority a visible next action and a place in the calendar. Include the file, person or decision needed to start.
Record the result when the work block ends. Use done, blocked or deliberately stopped, with a short explanation rather than a personal judgment.
Review the record before adding tools. Keep rules that helped you decide, and remove rules that made routine work harder to start.

sections.question: How are principles, rules and routines different?
sections.answer: Principles describe what matters, rules resolve recurring choices, and routines specify when you apply those rules. A principle might be reliable client delivery. Its rule might be to raise a deadline risk before accepting new work. The routine is the morning review of commitments. Keeping these layers distinct makes it easier to change a schedule without changing your values.

sections.question: How does an executive OS differ from a task manager?
sections.answer: A task manager stores work; an operating system explains how work is chosen and reviewed. A long list can be useful storage while still leaving you undecided each morning. Add a priority rule, a start condition and a review to the tool you already use. Moving the same unresolved list into another application does not resolve the underlying choices.

sections.question: What should an executive OS leave out?
sections.answer: Leave out rules you cannot apply and metrics that do not change a decision. A personal system does not need to reproduce a company dashboard. Avoid copying a founder’s schedule when your responsibilities differ. Keep sensitive business information in approved systems, and treat any AI summary as a draft requiring review rather than a source of authority.

guides.example: A delivery lead has an overdue client response and an appealing new project idea. The rule says to resolve an existing external commitment first. The next action becomes opening the response draft and identifying the unanswered question. The idea goes into a later-review list. At close, the lead records whether the response was sent or what specific information prevented it.

faq.question: Do I need an AI tool to use an executive OS?
faq.answer: No. A notebook, calendar and a short review record can carry the method. An AI assistant may help turn your notes into a proposed plan, but you still choose the priority, verify the facts and decide what may be shared. Start with the simplest place you will actually revisit.

faq.question: Where can I see what Spry sells?
faq.answer: The system manual page on the publisher’s main site describes the current product and purchase terms. Review that page before deciding whether the product fits your needs. This guide explains the planning method; it does not promise a particular financial, professional or personal result from using it.

faq.question: How do I know the system needs changing?
faq.answer: Change a rule when the review shows a recurring mismatch between the plan and the work you are responsible for. Record an example before revising it. If interruptions repeatedly displace the priority, change the start condition or capacity assumption rather than rebuilding the entire planning system after one difficult day.

guides.title: Reset cycle: restart a routine after a missed day
guides.definition: A reset cycle is a pattern of making an ambitious plan, missing part of it and abandoning the routine until a fresh start feels possible. A restart rule interrupts that pattern by defining the smallest useful action after a miss, so returning does not require clearing an accumulated backlog or redesigning the plan.
guides.best_for: people who repeatedly replace a useful routine because an imperfect week feels like a failed plan.
steps: Name the routine you stopped and the next occasion on which it would normally happen. Avoid using a symbolic future date as the only restart condition.
Remove obsolete catch-up work. Preserve real obligations and renegotiate deadlines with the people affected rather than silently dropping them.
Define a minimum action that still serves the routine’s purpose. Opening the current draft and adding the next sentence may be enough to restart writing.
Attach the action to a concrete cue, such as sitting down after breakfast. Make the materials available before that cue occurs.
At the next review, distinguish a missed action from an unsuitable plan. Adjust capacity when the same barrier keeps recurring.

sections.question: What is the difference between a restart and a redesign?
sections.answer: A restart resumes a useful routine at a manageable size; a redesign changes the routine because its purpose or constraints have changed. If you missed writing because of travel, reopening the draft may be sufficient. If the project was cancelled, writing to the old plan makes little sense. First decide whether the commitment still matters.

sections.question: Should you catch up on every missed task?
sections.answer: Catch up only on obligations that remain necessary. An overdue client delivery needs an explicit decision and communication. Unread optional articles do not automatically become debt. Review the backlog item by item, retain what still matters and remove what has expired. Adding all missed optional work to tomorrow often makes the return harder than the original routine.

sections.question: How can a restart rule stay realistic?
sections.answer: Make the rule small enough for a constrained day and specific enough to observe. A rule such as do better tomorrow does not tell you where to begin. A rule such as open the current proposal after the morning meeting does. If even the minimum is repeatedly impossible, the schedule or commitment needs review rather than stronger self-criticism.

guides.example: An operator misses the weekly review during a family disruption. Instead of rebuilding the dashboard or filling in every blank day, they open the current commitments list at the next available review. They identify one external deadline, contact its owner about the delay, and choose the next action. The gap stays visible without becoming a reason to abandon the record.

faq.question: Does restarting mean ignoring a missed deadline?
faq.answer: No. A restart rule is a planning aid, not permission to disregard commitments. Identify who is affected, explain the current state and agree on a feasible next step. Separating that obligation from optional catch-up work lets you address the consequence without carrying an undifferentiated backlog into every new day.

faq.question: What should a minimum viable day include?
faq.answer: Include the smallest action that preserves the purpose of your current priority, plus any obligation that cannot safely wait. This is a personal planning choice rather than a universal duration or quota. Write down what qualifies before a difficult day so you can apply the rule without renegotiating it under pressure.

faq.question: Is the reset cycle a medical diagnosis?
faq.answer: No. Spry uses reset cycle as a description of a planning pattern. It does not diagnose attention, mood or health conditions. If difficulty starting or maintaining routines is causing persistent distress or impairment, seek appropriate professional support rather than treating this organizational method as a replacement for care.

guides.title: Phone vortex meaning: interrupt the checking loop
guides.definition: A phone vortex is an informal description of a quick phone check expanding into an unplanned sequence of scrolling, notifications and app switching. The practical issue is the gap between why you picked up the phone and what happened next. A boundary makes the intended use explicit and gives you a stopping point.
guides.best_for: people whose phone checks interrupt work even when the phone also has legitimate uses during the day.
steps: Write the purpose before unlocking: answer a named person, find a specific address or check a calendar event. A purpose gives the check an endpoint.
Separate urgent contact from optional feeds. Configure permitted contacts using your device’s existing settings, checking that people who depend on you can still reach you.
Place the phone away from the working surface when it is not needed. Use an alternative clock or a written note if those are the reasons you keep reaching for it.
Keep a capture note for things you want to look up. Return to those questions at a chosen break rather than opening a browser for each thought.
When a check expands, close the app and return to a written next action. Record which cue pulled you away so the boundary can be changed.

sections.question: How is a phone vortex different from doomscrolling?
sections.answer: Doomscrolling refers to continued consumption of distressing news or similar negative material. A phone vortex is a broader informal label: it can include messages, shopping, entertainment or repeated checking without a clear endpoint. Naming the pattern helps identify the boundary to change; neither term by itself establishes a clinical condition.

sections.question: What if your work requires the phone?
sections.answer: Keep the required function available while separating it from optional activity. A service operator may need client calls but not social feeds during a scheduled work block. Decide which contacts and applications are necessary, test the setup, and review missed communications. The aim is to support your responsibilities rather than create a rigid rule that prevents you doing your job.

sections.question: What should you do immediately after an unplanned check?
sections.answer: Return to the next visible action of the task you left. If the action is unclear, write it before restarting. Do not spend the next work period calculating what the interruption says about your discipline. Capture the trigger once, change a relevant setting or location if appropriate, and use the next review to assess whether the change helped.

guides.example: A writer opens the phone to confirm a meeting time and then enters a news feed. The return rule is to close the feed, put the device on a shelf, and reopen the draft at the unfinished paragraph. Meeting alerts remain permitted. At review, the writer changes the calendar shortcut so checking an appointment does not start from a feed-filled home screen.

faq.question: Do you have to delete every distracting application?
faq.answer: No. Start with the boundary that addresses the actual interruption: location, alerts, entry point or an explicit end to the check. Deleting an application may be useful for some people, but it is an option rather than a prerequisite. Review whether the change supports the work and relationships you need the phone for.

faq.question: Should you make up the time lost to scrolling?
faq.answer: Do not automatically extend work into rest or other commitments. Reassess what remains feasible, finish the highest priority action and communicate any changed deadline. The purpose of recording the interruption is to improve the next boundary, not to create a punishment schedule that makes tomorrow harder to begin.

faq.question: Can this method treat compulsive phone use?
faq.answer: This guide offers organizational boundaries, not treatment. If phone use feels uncontrollable or is harming sleep, relationships or daily functioning, consider qualified support. A record of when checking occurs may help describe the problem, but an informal productivity label cannot establish its cause or replace an individual assessment.

guides.title: Personal scorecard: choose measures you can act on
guides.definition: A personal scorecard is a short record of actions and results used to decide what to change in a routine. It works best when each measure has a clear definition, a reliable place to record it and a review question. The purpose is to inform a decision, rather than assign a score to your worth.
guides.best_for: operators who collect plenty of metrics but cannot explain how those measures change the next week’s plan.
steps: Choose the decision the scorecard should support. For example, decide whether protected drafting time is sufficient for the current delivery commitment.
Define a controllable action and a relevant result separately. A completed drafting session and an accepted proposal describe different parts of the process.
Write what counts before recording. Specify whether preparing an outline counts as drafting, and avoid changing the definition midway through a comparison.
Record an observation where the work happens. Add a short note about a blocker when a count alone would mislead the review.
Review the pattern and select a change you can test. Retire any measure that consumes effort but never informs a choice.

sections.question: How do leading and outcome measures differ?
sections.answer: Leading measures describe activities you can influence directly, while outcome measures describe what those activities eventually produce. Drafting sessions are an activity; a client’s acceptance is an outcome influenced by other factors. Use both when they clarify the work, but do not assume a change in the activity caused a change in results without checking the context.

sections.question: What makes a personal KPI useful?
sections.answer: A useful indicator answers a decision question. If missed focused work repeatedly precedes delivery delays, recording interruptions may help you change the schedule. A total that rises without affecting a decision is less useful. Start with a small set you can interpret, and retain the definitions alongside the observations so comparisons mean the same thing over time.

sections.question: How should a scorecard handle a difficult week?
sections.answer: Keep the observation and add context instead of deleting the week or treating every missed target as a failure of character. Illness, caregiving and changing priorities can alter capacity. A review should decide whether the plan needs less work, a different cue or a renegotiated deadline. The scorecard supports that discussion; it cannot make the judgment for you.

guides.example: A consultant records protected drafting sessions, proposals sent and revisions requested. A week with many sessions but no proposal prompts a check of the completion rule: the drafts are being polished without a sending decision. The next experiment is an explicit review-and-send appointment. This is a worked planning example, not a claim that these indicators guarantee sales.

faq.question: How many measures should you start with?
faq.answer: Use only as many as you can define, record and review without displacing the work itself. There is no universal correct count. Begin with the decision you need to make, identify the observations necessary for it, and add another measure only when the existing record leaves a meaningful uncertainty.

faq.question: Should a personal scorecard include revenue?
faq.answer: It may include business outcomes when they matter to your responsibilities, but distinguish an outcome from an action you control. Revenue can change for reasons beyond the routine being reviewed. Avoid using the scorecard to promise earnings or treating a short trend as proof that a particular planning method caused the result.

faq.question: Can you share a team scorecard with individual details?
faq.answer: Share only information people are authorized to see and that is necessary for the review. Individual notes can contain sensitive context. Agree on definitions and access before collecting them, and avoid exporting a personal record into a broad dashboard by default. Organizational reporting should follow the applicable internal policies.

guides.title: Deep work: plan a focus block you can finish
guides.definition: Deep work is sustained attention on a demanding task with a defined outcome and limited avoidable interruption. A practical focus block specifies what you will produce, what materials you need and how you will resume after a disruption. It is a working arrangement to adapt to your responsibilities, rather than a universal schedule.
guides.best_for: people who reserve time for focused work but spend much of that time deciding where to begin.
steps: Name an output rather than a broad subject. Replace work on strategy with draft the options section for the upcoming decision meeting.
Open the required documents and identify missing information before the block. If a dependency is unavailable, choose a feasible portion of the work.
Agree on interruption boundaries with the people affected. Keep a way for genuinely urgent responsibilities to reach you.
Write the next action on a visible note before stepping away. Leave enough context that returning does not require reconstructing the whole problem.
Close by saving the output and stating what remains. Use the actual result to size the next block instead of assuming every calendar reservation was productive.

sections.question: How long should a focus block be?
sections.answer: Choose a duration that fits the task and your current responsibilities rather than copying a universal target. A block must leave room to start and close the work without ignoring care or service obligations. If you cannot sustain the planned interval, reduce its scope and record why before concluding that focused work is impossible for you.

sections.question: What should happen when an interruption is unavoidable?
sections.answer: Preserve a restart point and handle the interruption according to its importance. Write the open question, the next action and the location of the relevant material. A legitimate urgent request may need to replace the planned work entirely. Make that tradeoff visible in the record so an interrupted block does not silently look like completed capacity.

sections.question: How can teams protect focused time?
sections.answer: Agree on what counts as urgent, where requests should go and when a response is normally expected. A calendar label alone cannot resolve competing obligations. Teams can rotate coverage, batch nonurgent questions or schedule collaboration around concentration work, depending on their role. Check whether the arrangement helps both delivery and access before making it permanent.

guides.example: An analyst needs to compare contract options. Before the block, they open the current terms, identify the decision criteria and create the comparison table. A service escalation interrupts the analysis. The restart note names the unverified renewal clause and its document location. When the analyst returns, that note makes the next action visible without assuming the analysis was already finished.

faq.question: Is silence required for deep work?
faq.answer: No particular environment works for every person or task. Choose an arrangement that supports the output and accommodates the people around you. If noise is the actual barrier, change the location or agree on a boundary where feasible. If the barrier is an unresolved decision, a quieter room alone will not solve it.

faq.question: Should you track hours or completed work?
faq.answer: Track whichever observation helps the next planning decision, while recognizing their difference. Reserved hours show an allocation of capacity; a completed output shows what resulted. Reviewing them together can reveal scope or interruption problems. Avoid treating time at a desk as proof that a demanding task has progressed.

faq.question: Can AI do the focused work for you?
faq.answer: An AI assistant may help outline, summarize or suggest alternatives, but its output needs appropriate review. Keep confidential material in approved systems and verify any factual claim before relying on it. Decide which part of the task requires your judgment, then use tools to support that responsibility rather than obscure it.

guides.title: AI coaching at scale: define privacy and oversight
guides.definition: AI coaching at scale is the use of software-supported reflection and planning routines across a team or organization. A responsible rollout defines the purpose, permitted data, human oversight and reporting boundaries before inviting participants. Capabilities vary by product and contract, so privacy or effectiveness must be verified rather than assumed from a coaching label.
guides.best_for: team leads evaluating a bounded planning pilot rather than promising private, autonomous coaching to an entire workforce.
steps: Define a narrow use case such as preparing a weekly development reflection. Exclude employment decisions, clinical advice and other consequential judgments from the pilot.
Identify which information participants would enter. Remove customer details, confidential transactions and personal information that the approved environment does not permit.
Verify access, retention and reporting in the actual product and contract. Ask who can read raw conversations and whether administrators can export them.
Explain the pilot to participants, including its limitations and how to request human support. Do not describe conversations as private without verifying that claim.
Review useful planning actions and reported problems. Decide whether to change, stop or extend the pilot based on observed results and the organization’s policies.

sections.question: Can an employer assume aggregate reporting is anonymous?
sections.answer: No. Small groups, distinctive situations or combinations of fields can identify people even when names are removed. Review what the dashboard actually exposes and who can access it. A vendor’s aggregate-reporting label is not sufficient evidence of confidentiality. Set reporting boundaries through the organization’s approved privacy and security process before collecting coaching notes.

sections.question: Where should a human remain responsible?
sections.answer: A person should remain responsible for judgments affecting employment, safety, legal obligations and individual wellbeing. A planning assistant can prepare questions or summarize a participant’s own notes, but it cannot establish that an interpretation is correct. Define an escalation path and make clear that an automated response does not replace access to a manager or qualified professional.

sections.question: What should a pilot evaluation compare?
sections.answer: Compare the agreed use case with what actually happened: whether participants could complete a useful reflection, whether the proposed next actions were appropriate and what problems arose. Record the starting process so improvement claims have a basis. Do not infer effectiveness from adoption alone or turn a short internal pilot into a general claim about coaching outcomes.

guides.example: A team tests an assistant for voluntary weekly planning. Participants enter nonconfidential task descriptions and retain their own reflections. Before launch, the organizer checks administrator access and removes a proposed report that would expose distinctive personal notes. A human facilitator handles questions about workload and role conflict. The pilot evaluates the planning process rather than making decisions about employee performance.

faq.question: Does this guide recommend a particular coaching platform?
faq.answer: No. It describes questions to resolve before a rollout. Product capabilities, permissions and contract terms change, and a marketing description is not a verification. Evaluate the actual environment with your organization’s responsible reviewers and participants. The individual Spry planning manual is not evidence of enterprise privacy controls or workforce coaching effectiveness.

faq.question: Can coaching notes be used for performance decisions?
faq.answer: Do not silently repurpose reflections for a different use. Employees should understand the purpose and access boundaries before entering information. Any proposed employment use needs the organization’s applicable review and policy process. A model-generated interpretation should not be treated as an established fact about a person or their work.

faq.question: What if a participant asks for medical or legal help?
faq.answer: Provide the agreed route to an appropriate human resource or professional. Keep the assistant’s scope explicit and avoid presenting organizational prompts as clinical or legal advice. The pilot should have a clear way to stop or report unsuitable responses, with someone responsible for reviewing problems and changing the process.

guides.title: Executive coaching prompts: context to commitment
guides.definition: Executive coaching prompts are instructions for a structured reflection with an AI assistant about a work goal, decision or leadership situation. They provide relevant context, ask for questions before recommendations and end with an explicit next action. The assistant supports preparation and reflection; it does not become a qualified human coach or make decisions for you.
guides.best_for: leaders who want a reusable session structure instead of a long list of disconnected prompt tricks.
steps: State the decision or situation in neutral terms, removing information you are not authorized to share. Include the constraint that makes the issue difficult.
Ask the assistant to separate supplied facts, assumptions and unanswered questions before proposing a plan. Correct its interpretation before continuing.
Request one clarifying question at a time. Answer only what is relevant to the decision, and decline questions that would require confidential details.
Ask for feasible options and the tradeoffs for each. Verify claims about people, policy or external facts using an appropriate source.
Choose the next action yourself and record its owner and review condition outside the chat. An agreeable answer is not evidence that the action happened.

sections.question: What is a useful prompt for a difficult decision?
sections.answer: Try: Help me examine this decision using only the facts I supply. First identify my objective, constraints and uncertainties. Ask a clarifying question before suggesting options. For each option, name a tradeoff and an assumption I should verify. Finish by asking which next action I choose. This is an example structure, not a guarantee of reliable advice.

sections.question: How can a manager prepare a conversation?
sections.answer: Ask for open questions that would help you understand the situation rather than a diagnosis of the other person. A useful instruction is: Help me prepare a conversation about this missed commitment; separate my observations from interpretations and suggest questions about barriers and expectations. Review the suggestions yourself, and keep the actual conversation under human responsibility.

sections.question: How should you finish an AI reflection session?
sections.answer: End with a decision record that distinguishes what you know from what remains uncertain. State the next action, the person responsible and when or under what condition it will be reviewed. Save it in the system you actually use for commitments. Without that handoff, a well-written chat can become another place where plans are stored but never revisited.

guides.example: A founder is unsure whether to accept a new request while a delivery is late. The prompt asks for constraints and missing information before advice. The assistant’s proposed plan assumes a teammate is available; the founder corrects that assumption. The chosen action is to confirm delivery capacity before replying. The chat helps reveal a question, while the founder retains authority over the commitment.

faq.question: Can a prompt turn ChatGPT into an executive coach?
faq.answer: A prompt can shape a conversation, but it does not supply professional qualifications, personal accountability or verified knowledge about your situation. Treat the output as material to review. A human coach or other qualified adviser may be appropriate when the issue requires experience, a continuing relationship or responsibilities a software assistant cannot provide.

faq.question: Should you paste private meeting notes into a prompt?
faq.answer: Only use information that your approved environment and organizational policies permit. Remove unnecessary personal, customer and transaction details before preparing the prompt. Even a useful summary can expose confidential context. If you cannot determine whether the environment is approved for the material, use a nonconfidential description or keep the preparation outside the tool.

faq.question: What makes a prompt reusable?
faq.answer: A reusable prompt defines the session’s purpose, required context, questions, boundaries and ending. Keep those elements stable while replacing the situation-specific facts. After using it, check whether the session produced a clear action or revealed a missing fact. Revise the structure when it repeatedly produces generic advice or unsupported assumptions.

guides.title: Structure ChatGPT conversations for ongoing work
guides.definition: A structured ChatGPT conversation is a working thread with an explicit purpose, current context, agreed constraints and a clear handoff at the end. It separates exploration from decisions and records which facts still need checking. Structure helps you review the exchange without assuming the assistant remembers every detail or that its summary is accurate.
guides.best_for: people who revisit ongoing work in chat and find that the original constraints or decisions have become unclear.
steps: Start with a brief naming the task, the intended reader or user, the available material and the decision you need to make.
Ask the assistant to restate the constraints and identify missing information. Correct mistakes before requesting a long draft or plan.
Keep separate tasks in distinguishable sections or conversations. Put the relevant context in the current request instead of relying on an assumed memory.
Mark proposed actions as proposals until you have reviewed them. Keep a separate decision record for approved choices and unresolved questions.
Close with a handoff stating the current artifact, the next action and the facts requiring verification. Save the authoritative record in your normal work system.

sections.question: What belongs in a conversation brief?
sections.answer: Include enough context to interpret the task without copying unrelated material. State the purpose, constraints, source documents and what a useful output would look like. If the assistant must work from a particular document, provide the relevant approved content and distinguish it from your interpretation. Label uncertainty instead of inviting the model to fill gaps with plausible detail.

sections.question: How do you recover a conversation that has drifted?
sections.answer: Pause and write a fresh brief from the current facts. Identify which earlier decisions remain in force, which suggestions were rejected and what the next output should accomplish. Review the assistant’s restatement before continuing. A long conversation is not automatically a reliable record, so verify important details against the source rather than relying on a generated recap.

sections.question: Where should final decisions live?
sections.answer: Store final decisions in the system your work depends on: a project record, document or task manager with an identifiable owner. A chat may be useful for exploration, but its suggestions and revisions can make the final state ambiguous. Link the approved artifact from the handoff and state what is still unresolved so a later session starts from the right version.

guides.example: An operator uses a chat to develop a meeting brief. Early in the exchange, the deadline changes. Before drafting, the operator supplies the current deadline, the approved agenda and the unanswered questions in a new brief. After reviewing the draft, they save the approved document in the project workspace and close the conversation with a link and the remaining verification task.

faq.question: Does this structure guarantee that ChatGPT remembers context?
faq.answer: No. This is a method for making your own context and decisions explicit. Product behavior and available context vary, and an assistant may omit or misinterpret information. Provide the facts needed for the current task and verify the restatement. Do not rely on an assumed memory for a consequential deadline, instruction or commitment.

faq.question: Should every project use the same conversation?
faq.answer: Use whatever arrangement keeps the purpose and authoritative record clear. Separate unrelated work when mixing it would make constraints hard to follow. A shared project brief can carry the current context between sessions without preserving every message. The important test is whether you can identify the latest approved artifact and the next action.

faq.question: How should you handle a confident but unsupported answer?
faq.answer: Ask which supplied source supports the claim and verify it independently where needed. If no supporting source is available, label the statement as an assumption or remove it from the decision record. Confidence in the wording does not establish accuracy. Keep the question visible until an appropriate source or responsible person resolves it.
